summary:
Victoria's anti-vilification law, the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025. It inserts civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958, and repeals the Racial and Religious Tolerance Act. The stated aims are equal participation and public safety. The criminal provisions take effect on 30 June 2026 and cover vilification on the grounds of gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation, with a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment. Political, religious and academic exemptions apply, along with a further provision reported as the "Sam Kerr clause".

Gender identity has been a prohibited discrimination ground in Victoria since 2000, when the Equal Opportunity (Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation) Act 2000 amended the Equal Opportunity Act 1995; the ground was retained in the replacement Equal Opportunity Act 2010. Sex characteristics were added with effect from 2021. The Justice Legislation Amendment (Police and Other Matters) Bill 2022, passed in September 2022, extended protection on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds to on-duty Victoria Police officers.

Religious exemptions remain in the Equal Opportunity Act 2010. They allow religious organisations, including adoption and fostering agencies and charities that receive no government funding, to discriminate against and reject LGBT employees and clients. The Equal Opportunity (Religious Exceptions) Amendment Bill 2021, passed in December 2021 and effective 15 June 2022, bars religious schools and organisations from discriminating against employees because of sexual orientation, gender identity or marital status, and bars government-funded bodies from refusing services on those grounds except where conformity with doctrine is an inherent requirement, such as hiring a religious studies teacher.

Victoria recognises gender transition. Birth certificates are issued by the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and driver licences carry no recorded gender marker. Updated regulations in November 2025 removed all fees and costs for applications to change the sex recorded on a birth certificate. Earlier law required an applicant to be unmarried and to have undergone sexual reassignment surgery. Parliament removed the unmarried requirement early, in May 2018, ahead of its scheduled lapse in December 2018. An August 2016 bill that would have removed both requirements and allowed parents to alter a child's gender descriptor with the child's informed consent did not pass.

Conversion practices are prohibited. The Change or Suppression (Conversion) Practices Prohibition Bill passed the lower house 55-0 in December 2020 and the Legislative Council 27-9 on 5 February 2021, with penalties of up to approximately A$200,000 or up to 10 years' imprisonment, effective February 2022, one year after royal assent. The prohibition was preceded by the Health Complaints Act, from the Health Complaints Bill 2016 and effective 1 February 2017, which empowers the Health Complaints Commissioner to issue warnings and temporary or permanent bans; the commissioner opened an investigation in May 2018.

In August 2024 the Supreme Court of Victoria upheld the provision of puberty blockers to transgender children with stress and anxiety. In the same month a Victorian coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people. The state government says it is reviewing the recommendations, and local advocacy groups will press for their implementation.

Victoria is the only state with an LGBTIQA+ Commissioner. The inaugural Gender and Sexuality Commissioner, Ro Allen, was appointed in July 2015 to streamline federal and state laws so that passports and birth certificates align with affirmed gender and to strengthen workplace protections for transgender workers; the office was later renamed Commissioner for LGBTIQ+ Communities. Joe Ball, a transgender man, was appointed on 23 September 2024 for a three-year term to advise government on safe and inclusive policies, services and programmes and to lead implementation of Pride in our Future, Victoria's ten-year LGBTIQA+ equality plan.

Reported funding cuts risk a backlog at the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission, established in 1975.
tangentialFactors:
Victoria's criminal law history bears on how the current regime was reached. Buggery was a crime in Victoria from 1958 until December 1980, when the Hamer Liberal government's repeal passed 72-7 and took effect in March 1981. The death penalty remained on the books for sodomy until 1949. The equal age of consent was set at 18 and lowered to 16 by the Crimes (Sexual Offences) Act 1991. A loosely worded soliciting for immoral purposes clause enabled continued police harassment of homosexual men until the late 1980s, including entrapment mass arrests at Black Rock Beach reported in 1976. Any remaining legislation banning sex between consenting adults in private was removed by royal assent effective 1 March 2022 and in effect by May 2022.

HIV-specific offences were repealed. Intentional HIV transmission was singled out under section 19A of the Crimes Act, carrying up to 25 years' imprisonment against a 20-year maximum for manslaughter; the Crimes Amendment (Repeal of Section 19A) Act 2015 passed on 28 May 2015, received assent on 2 June 2015 and took effect immediately, with such conduct now dealt with as causing serious injury. An April 2022 Act repealed all HIV legislation on mandatory public health notifications, blood donations and human tissue services, effective 15 February 2023.

Sexual orientation has been a protected attribute in Victoria since 2000, retained in the Equal Opportunity Act 2010.
localsOnly:
Victoria operates an expungement scheme for historical homosexual offences that are no longer criminal. It passed on 15 October 2014 and took effect on 1 September 2015, allowing the individual or a representative of a deceased person to apply to the Secretary of the Department of Justice and Regulation. On a successful application the person may lawfully claim not to have been convicted, and the conviction does not appear on a police records check, avoiding travel and employment restrictions. Parliament issued a formal apology on 24 May 2016.

Domestic relationships have been registrable in Victoria since 1 December 2008 under the Relationships Act, passed on 10 April 2008.

Residents applying to change the sex recorded on a birth certificate do so through the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and since November 2025 no fees or costs apply to those applications.
outOfScopeNotes:
The August 2016 bill to remove the unmarried and surgery requirements for birth-certificate changes failed. The date on which the surgery requirement was later removed is not established by the source inventory.

The state government's response to the coroner's recommendations on health care for trans and gender-diverse people is described as under review; no implementation timeline is sourced.

The scale of the reported funding cuts at the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission and their effect on complaint handling are not quantified in the sources.

The scope of the provision reported as the "Sam Kerr clause" in the 2025 anti-vilification Act is not defined in the sources.

Several claims about Victoria's discrimination and vilification framework rest on a reference page rather than a live government or parliamentary document.
